title: Open-Market Buybacks: Taxing Your Gains and Investor Strategy

faq.q: What is an open-market share buyback?
faq.a: An open-market share buyback is when a company repurchases its own shares directly from the stock exchange, similar to how a regular investor buys shares. This contrasts with a tender offer, where the company makes a direct offer to shareholders.

faq.q: How does SEBI's reintroduction of open-market buybacks affect me?
faq.a: The reintroduction, effective August 1, 2026, primarily means that if you sell shares in such a buyback, any gains will be taxed as capital gains in your hands, either short-term or long-term, depending on your holding period.

faq.q: What are the tax implications of selling shares in an open-market buyback?
faq.a: Gains from selling shares in an open-market buyback are treated as capital gains. Short-Term Capital Gains (held for ≤ 12 months) are taxed at your slab rate. Long-Term Capital Gains (held for > 12 months) over ₹1 lakh are taxed at 10% without indexation.

faq.q: Is there a difference in taxation between open-market and tender offer buybacks?
faq.a: Yes. In tender offer buybacks, the company pays a tax (under Section 115QA), making the gains tax-exempt for the investor. In open-market buybacks, the investor is liable for capital gains tax.

faq.q: Should I sell my shares if a company announces an open-market buyback?
faq.a: The decision depends on factors like the buyback price relative to your cost, your holding period, your tax situation, and your long-term view of the company's prospects. It's essential to evaluate these aspects before making a choice.

faq.q: Will open-market buybacks lead to market manipulation?
faq.a: SEBI has put in place regulations to prevent market manipulation, such as limiting the daily purchase quantity and the overall duration of the buyback program. These measures aim to ensure fair play and transparency.
